 Tuesday's nationwide emergency alert test won't buzz your phone. Here's why 
 The Emergency Alert System (EAS) is a nationwide public alert system; FEMA must conduct a nationwide test of the warning system at least once every three years. 
 By Frank Heinz • 
 Published 1 hour ago • 
 Updated 37 minutes ago 
 BOOKMARKER 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 We’ve all heard it: the Emergency Alert System. That loud sound signifying a national emergency. But who decided to use that sound? And is it designed to be that annoying? 
 On Tuesday, Nov. 16, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will conduct a nationwide Emergency Alert System (EAS) test on TVs and radios but not mobile phones.
 The test will begin locally in North Texas at 1:20 p.m. and should take about a minute. After the test, TV and radio programming will return to normal. During the test, the message “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public," will be seen on the screen or read over the radio. The test message will include standard EAS alert tones for people who are deaf or hard-of-hearing.
 Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are
   WATCH HERE 
 Unlike the last test three years ago, FEMA said Tuesday's test will not include mobile phones . FEMA said it tested the Wireless Emergency Alerts system in 2023, but it will not be part of this year’s test, which assesses only the Emergency Alert System.
 The public does not need to take any action during the test.
 FEMA is required to conduct a nationwide test of the warning system at least once every three years.FEMA said the tests let it identify any trouble spots before the system is needed during an actual emergency.
 What is the Emergency Alert System?
 The Emergency Alert System (EAS) is a nationwide public alert system rolled out in 1997 that lets the President of the United States quickly alert Americans about a national emergency across various devices within 10 minutes.

 State and local agencies can also use EAS to provide important weather updates, such as tornado alerts or AMBER Alerts.
 Why is the alert sound so unpleasant?
 The EAS alert includes a sequence of loud noises meant to catch your attention, and it's intentionally loud and alarming. 
 Al Kenyon, FEMA IPAWS’s customer support brand chief, told NBC in 2023 that this distinctive sound educates the public to respond to alerts.
 “You know when you hear that sound, something important that may affect your life or property is going to follow,” he said.
 Former NBC journalist Raven Harper contributed to this story in 2023.
